newsitem.title: THAILAND: Battered Thai stocks, baht outlook bleak-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Battered Thai stocks, baht outlook bleak-analysts.

text.p: Thailand's battered stock market tumbled to a 35-month low on Friday after weeks of bad economic news, political uncertainty and rumours, and few analysts see it coming out of the depression soon.
The baht, which also came under assault on Friday after rumours by some Singapore investors that it may be devalued, had suffered a setback, they said.
The SET Index's closing 1.48 percent loss to 1007.51, its lowest level since October 1993 and just above the 1000 support level, unnerved analysts. The index has lost 8.9 percent since August 28.

Rumours that some brokerages may have been hit by client loan defaults sparked forced selling of stocks held by financially weak investors, especially locals, unable to meet margin payments, brokers said. The rumours began on Thursday.

However, news that a 15.7 billion baht (US$628 million) private sector rescue fund, operated by banks and brokers, had started buying shares to shore up the battered market helped cut losses by the close, analysts said.
"I need time to recover from the shock of seeing the index below 1,000 to forecast a new support level. It all looks very depressing," said Anucha Kulvisuth of First Asia Securities Plc.
Thai financial markets have this week been spooked by a Moody's Investors Service decision last Tuesday to downgrade Thailand's short-term debt ratings.

Other concerns were triggered by higher oil prices after a renewed U.S.-Iraq conflict, worries about sluggish Thai exports and an opposition-led no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Banharn Sila-archa due in parliament on September 18.

On Friday, the baht fell to 25.340-25.345 against the U.S. dollar at midday from 25.334-25.337 in early morning trade on heavy buying of the American currency, dealers said. It stabilised in late trading to 25.335-25.345.
The devaluation rumours, which were rife in late July, resurfaced because some offshore investors expected the baht to be devalued to help Thailand boost its sagging exports.
The Thai central bank denied the rumour but said it injected 14 billion baht into the money market to stabilise the currency on Friday.

"I just received a report about the rumour in Singapore. I want to stress that baht devaluation is not in any way planned by the bank," the Bank of Thailand spokeswoman Kleo-thong Hetrakul told Reuters.
A foreign exchange dealer said the pressure on the baht on Friday was not as heavy as in late July or early August on similar rumours.
"But it must be noted it is still an attack on the baht on a smaller scale, and the central bank's injection did little to ease the pressure," he said.
Nanthawat Chuaysong of Poonpipat Finance and Securities said, however, that rumoured problems involving brokerages were not entirely groundless.
The fact that investors were forced to sell shares at big losses to pay off debts showed this, he said. "These sort of problems start to come out in the media."
Somsak Boonsupaporn, marketing chief of United Securities, said he saw the Thai stock index's next technical support at between 950 and 980.
James Mitchell of Salomon Brothers added: "At some stage, people will start to come in to pick up bargains."
